name: Hashing, Signatures and HMAC
intent: Know which of a hash, a MAC (HMAC) and a digital signature proves what: that a message was not changed, that it came from someone holding a secret, or that it came from one particular party who cannot deny it.
scenario: A shop receives a webhook from a payment provider: id=evt77&order=1001&amount=500. The endpoint is public, so anyone can post to it. The shop must decide whether this request really came from the provider, whether it was changed on the way, and whether it is the same request that was already processed a minute ago.
problem: A hash of a message is public and anyone can recompute it, so it proves nothing about who sent the message. A tag built as hash(secret + message) looks like a fix, but with the common hash functions (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256) an attacker who sees one valid tag and knows or guesses the secret's length can extend the message and compute a valid tag for the longer one without knowing the secret. Even a correct HMAC can be undone by how it is checked: comparing the tags with a function that stops at the first difference leaks information, and a perfectly signed request can simply be sent again.

howItWorks.title: A hash proves integrity only against accidents
howItWorks.text: A hash function turns any input into a short fixed-size digest, and a good one makes it infeasible to find two inputs with the same digest. But there is no secret in it: whoever edits the message simply hashes the edited message and sends both. A hash next to the data protects against corruption and tells you a download matches a published digest, not against a person.

howItWorks.title: A MAC adds a shared secret: authenticity
howItWorks.text: A message authentication code is a tag that only someone holding the key can compute. HMAC is the standard construction: it hashes the message with the key mixed in twice (an inner and an outer hash). The receiver recomputes the tag with its copy of the key. If it matches, the message was not changed and came from a holder of the key. Because the key is shared, either side could have produced any valid tag.

howItWorks.title: hash(secret + message) is not an HMAC
howItWorks.text: Hashes like SHA-256 are built so that the digest is the internal state after the last block. An attacker who knows the digest of secret+message and the length of the secret can resume hashing from that state and obtain a valid tag for the original message followed by the hash's padding bytes and then data of their choice, without ever learning the secret. MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 and SHA-512 are affected; truncated variants such as SHA-384, and SHA-3 and BLAKE2, are not. HMAC's outer hash closes this hole. Use HMAC (or KMAC, the SHA-3 based MAC) through a library call rather than by composing hashes yourself.

howItWorks.title: A signature adds non-repudiation
howItWorks.text: A digital signature is made with a private key and checked with the matching public key. Anyone can verify it, but only the key holder could have made it, so the receiver cannot forge messages the sender never sent and the sender cannot easily deny one (as long as the private key was not stolen or shared). It costs more compute than a MAC and needs public keys that can be trusted and rotated. Use it when the verifier must not be able to forge, or when many parties verify.

howItWorks.title: Verify safely: constant time, and stop replays
howItWorks.text: Compare the received tag with the expected one using a constant-time comparison from your library, so the time taken does not reveal how many leading bytes were right. A valid signed request can still be captured and sent again: sign a timestamp together with the body, reject timestamps older than a few minutes, and remember the event ids already processed for that window. Make the handler idempotent as well, because honest providers retry.

pros: HMAC is fast, small, and a library call on every platform
A signature lets any number of parties verify without being able to forge
A timestamp plus a remembered id turns a signed request into a one-time request
None of them needs the message to be secret: a MAC needs a secret channel only for its key, a signature only an authentic copy of the public key
cons: A shared HMAC key must be stored by both sides, rotated, and never logged
HMAC cannot prove to a third party which side made a message
Signatures need key distribution, trust and rotation, and are slower
Signing the wrong bytes (parsed instead of raw body) makes verification fail or become bypassable
whenToUse: HMAC for webhooks, signed cookies and internal service-to-service requests where both ends are yours or agreed
A signature when one party issues something that many others must verify, or must not be able to forge (tokens, software releases, documents)
whenNotToUse: A plain hash as authentication, or hash(secret + message) as a MAC
A MAC when you need proof to an outsider that the other party sent it
Home-made schemes for passwords: use a slow password hash (see password-hashing)
pitfalls: Computing hash(secret + message), or hash(message + secret), instead of an HMAC
Comparing the tag with == or a string equals that stops at the first difference
Verifying a re-serialised body: sign and verify the exact raw bytes that were received
Signing the body but not the timestamp, so an old request is replayed with a fresh timestamp
Checking the timestamp window but not remembering ids, so a replay inside the window still works
Using one HMAC key for many purposes, or putting it in client code, so that every holder can forge

quiz.question: A team signs requests with tag = SHA-256(secret + body). An attacker sees one valid request, body and tag. What can they do without knowing the secret?
options: Nothing, because SHA-256 cannot be reversed and so the tag cannot be extended or forged
Append data to the body and compute a valid tag for the longer body
Recover the secret by hashing the body and subtracting
Change any single byte inside the existing body and still keep exactly the same tag
quiz.explanation: The digest is the hash's internal state after the last block, so the attacker can continue from it. This does not reveal the secret and does not let them edit existing bytes, but it forges an extended message (with a real hash such as SHA-256, the original padding bytes sit between the old body and the appended data). HMAC avoids it with a second, outer hash.

quiz.question: A partner disputes that they sent an order, and you need to prove to an arbitrator that the partner made it. You and the partner share an HMAC key. Why is the HMAC tag weak evidence?
options: HMAC tags are always too short to be unique, so two different orders collide
HMAC can be reversed with enough computing power to reveal who held the key
You hold the same key, so you could have produced the tag yourself
A tag cannot detect whether the order was edited after it was sent by anyone
quiz.explanation: A shared key makes both sides equally able to create valid tags, so the tag shows only that some key holder made it. A signature checked with the partner's public key can be made only by the private key holder. HMAC does detect edits, and its length is not the issue.

quiz.question: Your webhook handler verifies a correct HMAC over the body and a timestamp within 5 minutes. A captured request is replayed 20 seconds later and credits the order a second time. What is missing?
options: A longer HMAC key, because the replayed request carries a valid tag
Remembering processed event ids for the window, or making the handler idempotent
A stricter signature algorithm, for example a bigger hash with more output bits
Comparing the two tags with a plain equals check instead of a hash function
quiz.explanation: The replay is byte for byte the original, so its signature and timestamp are valid inside the window. Only state (seen ids) or an idempotent operation stops a second effect. A stronger hash or key does not change that, and a plain equals check makes things worse.
